\section{Why Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic cascade (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
We evaluate three independent probes on Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Re-prompting on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification yields P(yes) separation of $0.0006$ between gold and non-gold entities ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.779$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) marginally outperforms majority vote ($0.837$) without closing the oracle gap ($0.867$).

\paragraph{The asymmetry.}
Cross-sample frequency agreement achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.868$---the only effective entity-level signal---while all three self-verification probes fail.
Models encode entity-level quality in output \textit{distributions} (which entities recur across samples) rather than in per-sample self-evaluation capacity (whether the model can judge its own extractions).
This asymmetry---strong distributional signal, absent introspective signal---explains why entity-level construction succeeds (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}) while selection based on self-judgment does not.

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
4	These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
5	Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
6	The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
7	Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
8	This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for structured generation?
9	We investigate this question for NER and validate the core findings on SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.
10	
11	The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
12	Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
13	This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
14	We show this assumption fails.
15	Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
16	Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
17	Our diagnostic framework fills this gap: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) explain why strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.
18	
19	We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
20	Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC ($p{>}0.05$ for all comparisons).
21	Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$).
22	To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated seven approaches: entity self-judgment (ESJ), multi-round self-consistency (MRSC), latent-space aggregation (LSC), heterogeneous temperature sampling (Het-T), adaptive sampling budget (ASB), self-consistency distillation (SCD), and a supervised entity verifier.
23	All seven fail across three datasets and two model families.
24	ESJ achieves AUROC of 0.51 (indistinguishable from chance), while frequency-based agreement reaches 0.87.
25	MRSC produces $P(\text{yes})$ separation of 0.0006 between correct and incorrect entities.
26	The supervised verifier achieves entity-level AUC of 0.923 but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp F1, with negative cross-dataset transfer.
27	A hidden-state probe confirms that discriminative information exists in model representations but remains inaccessible through the prompt-based self-judgment interface.
28	
29	These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), a 4B ablation, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
30	We extend to Qwen3-72B in the zero-shot regime to test whether the capability ceiling persists at larger scale.
31	Cross-task validation on Spider SQL parsing (GPT-5.5, $n{=}196$) confirms the diagnostic cascade: degeneracy reaches 87.2\%, and the F1 failure mode dominates.
32	Our prescriptive analysis identifies three escape routes that work precisely because they bypass entity-level self-verification: entity-level construction via majority vote ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$; $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC, $p{=}0.004$), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and LP-based selection restricted to low-degeneracy regimes.

38	\label{fig:overview}
39	\end{figure*}

44	    A four-stage cascade (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) that identifies where and why self-consistency fails for structured generation, cross-task validated on NER and SQL parsing (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
45	
46	    \item \textbf{Impossibility evidence.}

48	
49	    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation.}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for structured generation?
We investigate this question for NER and validate the core findings on SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.

The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
We show this assumption fails.
Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
Our diagnostic framework fills this gap: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) explain why strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.

We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC ($p{>}0.05$ for all comparisons).
Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$).
To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated seven approaches: entity self-judgment (ESJ), multi-round self-consistency (MRSC), latent-space aggregation (LSC), heterogeneous temperature sampling (Het-T), adaptive sampling budget (ASB), self-consistency distillation (SCD), and a supervised entity verifier.
All seven fail across three datasets and two model families.
ESJ achieves AUROC of 0.51 (indistinguishable from chance), while frequency-based agreement reaches 0.87.
MRSC produces $P(\text{yes})$ separation of 0.0006 between correct and incorrect entities.
The supervised verifier achieves entity-level AUC of 0.923 but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp F1, with negative cross-dataset transfer.
A hidden-state probe confirms that discriminative information exists in model representations but remains inaccessible through the prompt-based self-judgment interface.

These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), a 4B ablation, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
We extend to Qwen3-72B in the zero-shot regime to test whether the capability ceiling persists at larger scale.
Cross-task validation on Spider SQL parsing (GPT-5.5, $n{=}196$) confirms the diagnostic cascade: degeneracy reaches 87.2\%, and the F1 failure mode dominates.
Our prescriptive analysis identifies three escape routes that work precisely because they bypass entity-level self-verification: entity-level construction via majority vote ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$; $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC, $p{=}0.004$), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and LP-based selection restricted to low-degeneracy regimes.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Diagnostic framework.}
    A four-stage cascade (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) that identifies where and why self-consistency fails for structured generation, cross-task validated on NER and SQL parsing (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

    \item \textbf{Impossibility evidence.}
    Seven entity-level methods $\times$ three NER datasets $\times$ two model families all fail to close the correlation-selection gap, constituting systematic evidence for a capability ceiling in entity-level self-verification (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}).

    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation.}
    Hidden-state probing reveals that discriminative information exists in model representations (frequency agreement AUROC${=}0.87$) but the prompt-based self-judgment interface cannot access it (ESJ AUROC${=}0.51$), identifying an introspection limit rather than an information deficit (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

    \item \textbf{Prescriptive escape routes.}
    Entity-level construction ($+1.02$\,--\,$1.40$\,pp), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and regime-specific LP selection ($+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD) succeed because they bypass entity-level self-verification.
    A degeneracy decomposition $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1] = (1{-}D) \cdot G_{\text{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ yields a critical threshold $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$ above which self-consistency cannot yield meaningful improvement (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with selection or aggregation---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where standard aggregation mechanisms break down.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks across fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B and zero-shot 72B models.
4	All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL-2003, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
5	For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
6	We identify a diagnostic cascade---instance degeneracy sets the ceiling on improvement, oracle headroom determines the opportunity, and LP compression limits exploitation---that persists under our 72B zero-shot configuration, providing, to our knowledge, the first systematic characterization of when test-time scaling succeeds or fails for NER and similar set-valued extraction tasks.
7	The diagnostic motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.006$, construction family $k{=}10$) and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$, $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.20$) under fine-tuning. Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a degeneracy decomposition confirms that SC gain vanishes when degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
8	\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with selection or aggregation---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where standard aggregation mechanisms break down.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks across fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B and zero-shot 72B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL-2003, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We identify a diagnostic cascade---instance degeneracy sets the ceiling on improvement, oracle headroom determines the opportunity, and LP compression limits exploitation---that persists under our 72B zero-shot configuration, providing, to our knowledge, the first systematic characterization of when test-time scaling succeeds or fails for NER and similar set-valued extraction tasks.
The diagnostic motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.006$, construction family $k{=}10$) and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$, $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.20$) under fine-tuning. Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a degeneracy decomposition confirms that SC gain vanishes when degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, yet for structured information extraction (IE), where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, a persistent gap separates quality estimation from sample selection.
We ask whether entity-level agreement signals can bridge this gap.
Across seven methods spanning self-judgment, self-refinement, latent consistency, heterogeneous verification, adaptive budgeting, distillation, and supervised classification, we find that no entity-level agreement signal reliably improves selection for named entity recognition (NER), relation extraction (RE), or Text-to-SQL.
The failure is systematic: all signals yield null or negative selection gains on four RE benchmarks and SQL parsing (87.2\% output degeneracy).
A temperature ablation reveals agreement becomes actively misleading under elevated sampling (conditional $\rho{=}{-}0.048$ on Few-NERD), and a mechanistic probe identifies a gap between hidden-state frequency agreement (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] 0.87) and prompt-based self-evaluation (AUROC 0.51), an introspection boundary that surface agreement cannot cross.
These negative results delineate where self-consistency (SC) does succeed for IE: through paths that bypass entity-level agreement.
Log-probability selection improves F1 by $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.019$), entity-level construction via weighted voting gains $+1.02$\textendash$1.40$\,pp, and cross-model ensembles add $+0.42$\,pp.
Each exploits sequence-level or cross-model signals rather than entity-level self-verification.
A degeneracy decomposition confirms SC gain vanishes once output degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
\end{abstract}
%% REFRAME: scope precision + empirical exhaustion methodology

\section{Why Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic cascade (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
We evaluate three independent probes on Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Re-prompting on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification yields P(yes) separation of $0.0006$ between gold and non-gold entities ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.779$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) marginally outperforms majority vote ($0.837$) without closing the oracle gap ($0.867$).

\paragraph{The asymmetry.}
Cross-sample frequency agreement achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.868$---the only effective entity-level signal---while all three self-verification probes fail.
Models encode entity-level quality in output \textit{distributions} (which entities recur across samples) rather than in per-sample self-evaluation capacity (whether the model can judge its own extractions).
This asymmetry---strong distributional signal, absent introspective signal---explains why entity-level construction succeeds (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}) while selection based on self-judgment does not.

%% If hidden state probe AUROC ≈ MV (0.87) while ESJ AUROC = 0.51,
%% this confirms information exists in representations but the
%% prompt-based self-judgment interface cannot access it.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for structured generation?
We investigate this question for NER and validate the core findings on SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.

The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
We show this assumption fails.
Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
Our diagnostic framework fills this gap: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) explain why strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.

We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC ($p{>}0.05$ for all comparisons).
Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$).
To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated seven approaches: entity self-judgment (ESJ), multi-round self-consistency (MRSC), latent-space aggregation (LSC), heterogeneous temperature sampling (Het-T), adaptive sampling budget (ASB), self-consistency distillation (SCD), and a supervised entity verifier.
All seven fail across three datasets and two model families.
ESJ achieves AUROC of 0.51 (indistinguishable from chance), while frequency-based agreement reaches 0.87.
MRSC produces $P(\text{yes})$ separation of 0.0006 between correct and incorrect entities.
The supervised verifier achieves entity-level AUC of 0.923 but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp F1, with negative cross-dataset transfer.
A hidden-state probe confirms that discriminative information exists in model representations but remains inaccessible through the prompt-based self-judgment interface.

These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), a 4B ablation, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
We extend to Qwen3-72B in the zero-shot regime to test whether the capability ceiling persists at larger scale.
Cross-task validation on Spider SQL parsing (GPT-5.5, $n{=}196$) confirms the diagnostic cascade: degeneracy reaches 87.2\%, and the F1 failure mode dominates.
Our prescriptive analysis identifies three escape routes that work precisely because they bypass entity-level self-verification: entity-level construction via majority vote ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$; $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC, $p{=}0.004$), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and LP-based selection restricted to low-degeneracy regimes.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Diagnostic framework.}
    A four-stage cascade (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) that identifies where and why self-consistency fails for structured generation, cross-task validated on NER and SQL parsing (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

    \item \textbf{Impossibility evidence.}
    Seven entity-level methods $\times$ three NER datasets $\times$ two model families all fail to close the correlation-selection gap, constituting systematic evidence for a capability ceiling in entity-level self-verification (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}).

    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation.}
    Hidden-state probing reveals that discriminative information exists in model representations (frequency agreement AUROC${=}0.87$) but the prompt-based self-judgment interface cannot access it (ESJ AUROC${=}0.51$), identifying an introspection limit rather than an information deficit (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

    \item \textbf{Prescriptive escape routes.}
    Entity-level construction ($+1.02$\,--\,$1.40$\,pp), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and regime-specific LP selection ($+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD) succeed because they bypass entity-level self-verification.
    A degeneracy decomposition $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1] = (1{-}D) \cdot G_{\text{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ yields a critical threshold $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$ above which self-consistency cannot yield meaningful improvement (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}).
\end{enumerate}
